h1: Visiting Munich beer halls and beer gardens as a first timer
title: Munich Beer Halls for First-Timers | Craft Beer School
desc: A first-timer's guide to Munich beer halls and beer gardens: how seating, ordering, self-service and bringing your own food work.
teaser: In a traditional Munich beer garden you can bring your own picnic. Few visitors know that.
standfirst: Munich's beer halls and beer gardens have their own habits. Knowing a few of them, from shared tables to the glass deposit, makes a first visit far more relaxed.
sections: Beer halls and beer gardens are different places

A beer hall is a large indoor space with long tables, table service and often a brass band. A beer garden is outdoors under chestnut trees, open in the warmer months and often partly self-service. Both serve Munich's own breweries, mostly helles, dunkel and wheat beer. Both are built for sitting a long time.

Munich has six big breweries whose beer you will see everywhere: Augustiner, Hacker-Pschorr, Hofbräu, Löwenbräu, Paulaner and Spaten. Each runs or supplies its own halls and gardens. A good first trip samples a few.

Tables are shared. If there is space on a bench, ask "Ist hier frei?" (is this free?) and sit down. Nobody expects you to wait for an empty table. Some tables carry a sign saying they are reserved or kept for regulars, called a Stammtisch. Leave those alone.

In big beer halls, a table of six or more may need a reservation at busy times. A couple or a small group can usually find space by walking around, especially in the afternoon.

The classic Munich serve is the Mass, a one litre glass. Many places also offer a half litre. Wheat beer usually comes in a half litre glass. A litre of 5% helles carries a fair amount of alcohol and warms up before you finish it, so a half litre is often the better order.

In table service areas you order from the server and usually pay them directly in cash or by card. Keep some euros on you. Rounding up the bill is the normal way to tip. Our guide on why beer tastes sweeter as it warms explains why a litre glass tastes different at the bottom.
Beer garden self-service and the deposit

Many beer gardens have a self-service section, the Selbstbedienung. You pick up a tray, collect food from the stalls, then join the queue for beer. Glasses often carry a deposit, the Pfand, added to the price. Return the glass to the rack to get it back, or keep the token if they use one.

Look for the tap station where staff fill glasses from a wooden barrel or a tap line. Lines move fast. Know what you want before you reach the front.
Yes, you can bring your own food

Traditional Bavarian beer gardens allow guests to bring their own food to the self-service area. Locals turn up with bread, cheese, radish and cold meats on a tablecloth. Tables with cloths or table service are for buying food from the garden. You still buy your drinks from the garden. Check each garden's own rules, since practice varies.

This makes beer gardens a good option for vegetarian travellers from India. Pick up bread, pretzels, cheese and salads from a supermarket and buy beer on site.

If you do order, Bavarian classics include the large soft pretzel (Brezn), obatzda (a spiced cheese spread), roast chicken and Weisswurst, a white veal sausage traditionally eaten before noon. Radi, thinly sliced white radish with salt, is a common snack with beer.

Vegetarian options exist but are fewer in traditional places: obatzda, cheese spaetzle, pretzels and salads are the usual choices.
What to drink in which season

Munich's beer calendar shapes what you will find on tap. Spring brings strong bock beers and, in Lent, the even stronger doppelbock, a malty lager often around 7 to 8% ABV with a name ending in "-ator". Summer is the beer garden season, with helles and wheat beer in the sun. Late September and early October bring Oktoberfest, when the big breweries serve a golden festival lager, the Festbier, usually around 6%.

In winter the beer gardens close or quieten and life moves indoors to the halls. Dunkel, the dark Munich lager with bread crust and light cocoa notes, suits the cold. If you can visit twice in different seasons, you will taste a different city.

Doppelbock and Festbier are stronger than they taste. Treat a litre of either with respect. See our guide to planning a first Oktoberfest trip if you are going in festival season.
Taste the house styles side by side

The pleasure of Munich is comparing the same style from different breweries. Order a helles in one hall and another the next day. Notice the bread and honey malt, the soft bitterness and how clean each finishes. Our guide to visiting a brewery taproom has tips on tasting in busy places.

Telling those helles apart is harder than it sounds. Lager differences are small and need a trained palate. Pace yourself, drink water and never drive afterwards.

Your first step: learn the phrase "Ist hier frei?" and pick two halls from different breweries for your first day.
faqs: Can you bring food to a Munich beer garden?
In traditional Bavarian beer gardens you can usually bring your own food to the self-service area, but drinks must be bought there. Check each garden's rules.
A Mass is a one litre glass of beer, the classic serve in Munich beer halls and gardens. Many places also serve half litres.
Do I need a reservation for a Munich beer hall?
Small groups can usually find space on shared benches. Larger groups at busy times should reserve a table.
